lessonData.subject: Mathematics / Algebra
lessonData.tagline: Unpack algebraic expressions by reversing the distributive law with precision.
lessonData.overview: Factorisation transforms an algebraic sum into a compact product by identifying and extracting the Highest Common Factor (HCF) from every term. Mastering this skill involves recognizing common numerical and variable powers while keeping careful track of negative signs inside brackets.

diagram.title: Steps to Complete Factorisation
diagram.description: The sequential logical flow for identifying and extracting the complete HCF from algebraic expressions.

nodes.label: Inspect Individual Terms
nodes.details: Break down each term into prime numerical factors and variable powers (e.g., in 6x² + 15x, look at 6, 15, x², and x).

nodes.label: Determine Complete HCF
nodes.details: Multiply the greatest common divisor of coefficients with each shared variable raised to its lowest exponent.

nodes.label: Assess Leading Signs
nodes.details: If the leading term or all terms are negative, pull out a negative sign and flip every sign inside the bracket.

nodes.label: Divide & Construct Brackets
nodes.details: Divide each original term by the extracted HCF to determine the remaining terms inside the brackets.

nodes.label: Check by Expansion
nodes.details: Use the distributive law to multiply back out and confirm you arrive at the exact starting expression.

chalkNotes.title: Extracting the Highest Common Factor (HCF)
chalkNotes.subtitle: Factorisation is the reverse of Expansion: ab + ac = a(b + c)
chalkNotes.coreRuleOrFormula: a · b + a · c = a(b + c)   and   -x - y = -(x + y)
bulletPoints: Always extract the HIGHEST Common Factor: both numbers and all shared variables to their lowest power.
Incomplete factorisation trap: Factoring 6x² + 15x as 3(2x² + 5x) leaves an unextracted variable 'x'. Full answer: 3x(2x + 5).
Negative sign rule: Factoring out a negative factor changes every sign inside brackets: -15x - 6 = -3(5x + 2).
Verify your work: Mentally expand your final answer using the distributive law to confirm it matches the original expression.
keyTakeaways: A factorisation is complete only when the terms inside the bracket share no further common factors besides 1.
Dividing a negative term by a negative factor yields a positive term.

quiz.question: Which of the following represents the completely factorised form of the expression: -10ax + 25ay?
quiz.explanation: To factorise completely: The numerical HCF of 10 and 25 is 5, and both terms share the variable 'a'. Factoring out 5a gives 5a(-2x + 5y), which is standardly written with the positive term first as 5a(5y - 2x). Option B extracts only the number 5, leaving common variable 'a' inside. Option C incorrectly handles signs because -5a(2x + 5y) expands to -10ax - 25ay, not +25ay. Option D leaves the common numerical factor 5 unextracted.

suggestedQuestions: Prerequisite Check: What is the HCF of 18a²b and 24ab²?
Misconception Probe: Why is writing -15x - 6 = -3(5x - 2) incorrect, and how does expanding it reveal the mistake?
Challenge Question: How do we factorise completely when an expression contains three terms, like 12x³ - 18x² + 6x?

factorisation-by-extracting-common-facto.title: Factorisation by Extracting Common Factors
factorisation-by-extracting-common-facto.description: Step-by-step process of identifying the highest common factor and writing an algebraic expression in factored form.

nodes.label: Original Expression
nodes.details: Examine all terms in the polynomial to inspect both numerical coefficients and variable powers.

nodes.label: Find the HCF
nodes.details: Determine the greatest common divisor of the numbers and the lowest exponent of shared variables.

nodes.label: Divide Each Term
nodes.details: Divide every term in the original expression by the HCF to determine what remains inside the bracket.

nodes.label: Factored Form
nodes.details: Express the result as the HCF multiplied by the quotient terms enclosed in parentheses.

key-properties-of-factorisation-by-extra.title: Properties of Factorisation by Common Factors
key-properties-of-factorisation-by-extra.description: Visualises the essential rules and mathematical properties used when extracting common factors from algebraic expressions.

nodes.label: Reverse Distributive Law
nodes.details: Factorisation reverses multiplication by placing the shared factor outside parentheses while keeping expression value unchanged.

nodes.label: Highest Common Factor (HCF)
nodes.sublabel: GCD of Coefficients & Lowest Variable Powers
nodes.details: The extracted monomial must take the largest numerical divisor and the smallest exponent of each variable common to all terms.

nodes.label: Bracketed Quotient
nodes.details: Terms remaining inside parentheses are computed by dividing each individual original term by the extracted common factor.

nodes.label: Term Count Invariance
nodes.sublabel: n terms outside → n terms inside
nodes.details: The number of terms inside the bracket must equal the number of terms in the original expression, preserving a 1 when a term equals the HCF.

real-world-applications-of-factorisation.title: Real-World Uses of Common Factor Extraction
real-world-applications-of-factorisation.description: How pulling out a greatest common factor simplifies everyday calculations in retail, construction, and wages.

nodes.label: Distributive Law in Reverse
nodes.details: Factoring out a shared variable groups operations together, cutting down the number of separate multiplication steps required.

nodes.label: Bulk Invoicing & Sales Tax
nodes.details: Stores apply the common sales tax rate to the combined price sum instead of computing tax on each product individually.

nodes.label: Fencing & Border Layouts
nodes.details: Contractors factor out shared dimensions to quickly determine combined border lengths and material requirements.

nodes.label: Shared Wage Payroll
nodes.details: Managers multiply an identical hourly pay rate by total combined hours rather than tallying each shift separately.

steps.name: Establish expansion
steps.caption: Expansion turns a product into a sum by multiplying terms.

steps.name: Define factorisation
steps.caption: Factorisation is the reverse; it pulls the common factor out of the sum.

steps.name: Identify the HCF
steps.caption: Look for the highest number and variable that divides into every part.

contrast:partial-factorisation-missing-v.title: Factorisation: Finding the Full HCF
contrast:partial-factorisation-missing-v.why: This visual comparison demonstrates that partial factorisation leaves a common variable trapped, whereas full factorisation extracts all shared factors to reach the simplest form.
contrast:partial-factorisation-missing-v.checkQuestion: Looking at the expressions inside the brackets, why is 3x(2x + 5) more 'complete' than 3(2x² + 5x)?

steps.name: Testing the rule
steps.caption: If we only factor out the numerical HCF, we get 3(2x² + 5x).

steps.name: Finding the leftover
steps.caption: Notice that both 2x² and 5x still share an x.

steps.name: Completing the step
steps.caption: To factorise completely, we extract the variable x too: 3x(2x + 5).

contrast:partial-factorisation-missing-v.focus: Extracting only a numerical factor and leaving common variable factors inside, resulting in incomplete factorisation.

contrast:neg-factor-sign-error.title: Testing the negative factor sign change
contrast:neg-factor-sign-error.why: It shows that expanding the result reveals why signs must change, transforming a silent sign error into a visible algebraic mismatch.
